target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety
objection: AI’s promised benefits do not outweigh its real-world costs: it creates economic insecurity by automating jobs and concentrating profits, undermines critical thinking by encouraging people to outsource reasoning, reproduces and amplifies racial bias, and poses major privacy risks through profiling and surveillance.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is inherently bad because of jobs, critical thinking, bias, and privacy harms
objection: Those harms do not make AI inherently bad; they are risks that can be reduced through responsible deployment, including reskilling, learning-oriented uses, fairness auditing, data minimization, and privacy-preserving techniques.

target: AG1’s assumption that guardrails can reliably make AI socially beneficial
objection: Guardrails are unlikely to keep up in practice because governance is structurally hard: deployment is fast, vendors disclose little, and incentives reward rapid rollout, so “responsible use” often fails at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that governance cannot keep up and therefore AI is not good overall
objection: Governance is not all-or-nothing; risk-tiered regulation, enforceable requirements, liability, and existing labor/consumer/safety institutions can make AI deployment practical and proportionate to risk.

target: AG1’s argument that risk-tiered regulation and accountability can solve AI harms
objection: Even risk-tiered regulation is undermined by proprietary opacity, rollout speed, uneven enforcement across jurisdictions, and competitive pressure, making it unreliable where harms are worst.

target: AG2’s claim that governance cannot keep up with AI harms
objection: Those are deployment challenges, not reasons to reject AI overall; governments and institutions can restrict high-risk uses, require ongoing monitoring, and even use AI to improve oversight and fairness auditing.

target: AG1’s claim that AI-based auditing and restricted high-risk uses can adequately control harms
objection: AI used for auditing can inherit the same bias and opacity problems, “high-risk” boundaries are easy to evade because many harmful uses look low-risk at first, and regulation can be captured or weakened by industry influence.

target: AG2’s claim that even human-in-the-loop review and due process cannot prevent AI harms
objection: AI can be deployed as decision support rather than autonomous decision-making, with human final review, contestability, and traceable records so that due process and accountability reduce harm.

target: AG1’s belief that human review and appeals will meaningfully constrain AI harms
objection: Human-in-the-loop often becomes rubber-stamping because of automation bias, appeals fail when proprietary systems cannot explain decisions, and accountability is diffused across humans and models.

target: AG2’s claim that human review and appeals are ineffective
objection: These problems are design-and-incentive issues, not reasons to reject AI; uncertainty thresholds, usable explanations, and audit trails can reduce automation bias and preserve accountability.

target: AG1’s claim that improved workflows, explanations, and audit trails can solve the harms
objection: In practice, appeals are inaccessible to most people because they require time, expertise, and often legal help, enforcement costs are easily absorbed by firms, and AI use structurally encourages cognitive offloading that weakens critical thinking.

target: AG2’s claim that the worst harms cannot be reliably prevented
objection: Rather than trying to govern every use perfectly, society can prioritize low- and medium-risk, high-value AI applications and postpone or restrict the most dangerous uses, capturing benefits while limiting exposure to the hardest harms.

target: AG1’s portfolio strategy that expands safer uses while restricting high-risk ones
objection: That strategy fails because AI systems and platforms are easily repurposed and expanded into riskier contexts, even supposedly low-risk uses can still create privacy and bias harms, and business incentives push firms toward the most profitable high-stakes deployments.

target: AG2’s claim that spillover and repurposing make a safer portfolio approach impossible
objection: Purpose limits, data governance, technical and organizational isolation, and gated approvals can be enforced to prevent spillover and repurposing, allowing beneficial uses while constraining risky expansion.

target: AG1’s claim that purpose limits, isolation, and gated approvals can stop spillover
objection: Those safeguards are hard to enforce consistently: firms can reinterpret purposes, technical isolation is not absolute, gates depend on vendor-controlled disclosure, and privacy harms also arise from breaches, memorization, and inference even without repurposing.

target: AG2’s claim that AI cannot be good overall because safeguards are too hard to enforce
objection: AI can also strengthen society’s defenses against misinformation and low accountability by providing provenance tools, authentication, and adaptive tutoring that improves verification skills and learning.

target: AG1’s claim that provenance tools and tutoring can offset AI’s harms
objection: Provenance and watermarking are easy to evade or strip, generation outpaces detection in an arms race, and tutoring systems still encourage cognitive offloading rather than independent checking.

target: AG2’s argument that AI harms outweigh benefits and that broad rejection is acceptable
objection: Rejecting AI would eliminate real, immediate benefits in accessibility, health, workplace safety, and education; a better approach is to expand demonstrably useful applications while tightening controls on high-risk ones.

target: AG1’s claim that society can keep the benefits while steering away from the harms
objection: The tradeoff is artificial because many useful functions can be provided by non-generative or privacy-preserving alternatives, and the same platform that delivers benefits also carries the privacy, bias, and automation risks that scale through reuse and incentives.
